schema.prerequisites: lesson ids that unlock this one
schema.try_it: browser exercise users do, not just read

lessons.plain_def: A large AI model trained on huge amounts of text so it can understand and generate language — predicting the next token, over and over, until it writes a full answer.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: The 2017 Transformer paper unlocked modern LLMs; consumer chatbots like ChatGPT (Nov 2022) made “talking to a model” mainstream.

try_it.title: Be the model for one step
try_it.prompt: Given the unfinished sentence “The cat sat on the ___”, pick the next word a language model is most likely to choose — and say why a model thinks in next-token guesses, not full essays at once.
try_it.debrief: LLMs don’t “know the answer” first — they keep picking the next token. Everyday phrases score high; weird ones score low.

quiz.q: What does an LLM mainly do, step by step?
choices: Search the whole internet for one perfect page
Predict the next token again and again to build an answer
Store every book as a searchable database
Run only if you install Python locally

quiz.q: Which event is tied to unlocking modern LLMs (per verified glossary)?

lessons.plain_def: The small chunks an AI model actually reads and writes — often pieces of words, not whole words. Models bill and limit context by token count, not by character count.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Subword tokenization (BPE era ~2015–2016) stuck; once commercial LLM APIs priced by the token (~2020+), every prompt, limit, and bill became a token problem.

try_it.title: Guess the token count
try_it.prompt: Split these into likely tokens (pieces, not always whole words): “ChatGPT”, “n8n”, “hallucinating”. Which one probably burns more tokens than it looks?
try_it.hint: Weird spellings and long rare words often split into more pieces.
try_it.debrief: Billing and context windows count tokens, not characters — so “short” text can still be expensive or fill the window fast.

quiz.q: What do LLM APIs usually bill and limit by?
A token is best described as…
choices: A small chunk the model reads/writes — often a piece of a word
A type of neural network layer

lessons.plain_def: A defined way for one program to talk to another — a contract of requests and responses — so apps can share data and features without sharing their internal code.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: APIs are decades-old computing glue; in AI products, “the API” usually means the HTTP endpoints you call to send prompts and get model output — how apps ship LLM features without training their own model.

try_it.title: Call a fake AI API
try_it.prompt: Fill a mini request: method POST, path /v1/chat, body {"prompt": "Say hi"}. Then match it to the response shape you’d expect back (text + usage).
steps: Read a sample JSON response and spot where the model text lives
try_it.debrief: You never see the model’s internals — you only honor the contract: send a valid request, parse the response.

choices: A contract of requests/responses so programs can talk without sharing internal code

quiz.q: In AI products, “the API” usually means…
choices: HTTP endpoints to send prompts and get model output
The physical power cord of a server

lessons.plain_def: Anthropic’s family of AI assistants and models — chat + API — trained to be helpful, honest, and harmless. You use it in the Claude apps or call it from your own software.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Anthropic introduced Claude publicly on Mar 14, 2023; the lineup later expanded (Haiku / Sonnet / Opus and later generations), so “Claude” became both a chat product and an API model family.

try_it.title: Chat app vs API
try_it.prompt: Same ask (“Summarize this paragraph”). Pick which channel fits: Claude chat app for a human tinkering once, or Claude API for your own app calling it in code.

scenarios.label: You want a quick summary in a browser tab
Your Next.js site needs summaries for every user

try_it.debrief: Claude is both a product you talk to and models you call — same family, different doors.

choices: In Claude apps and/or by calling it from your own software
Only if you fine-tune on a laptop GPU

lessons.plain_def: xAI’s conversational AI assistant — chat, search, voice, and creation tools — built to answer with real-time context and a less-filtered style than many rivals.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: xAI announced Grok on Nov 3–4, 2023 (early beta/waitlist); later it showed up via X Premium tiers, grok.com, and mobile apps — putting another big-lab assistant in the consumer mix.

try_it.title: Same question, two labs
try_it.prompt: You need an assistant with real-time context and a less-filtered style (per verified def). Tag which product fits that brief: Claude or Grok — and name the lab behind it.
try_it.debrief: Same job class (LLM assistants), different labs and product bets — Grok is xAI’s.

quiz.q: Per the verified definition, Grok is positioned as…
choices: A conversational AI with chat, search, voice, and creation tools

lessons.plain_def: An AI system where the model itself decides what to do next — picking tools, looping on a goal — instead of only answering inside a fixed, pre-written script.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Agent/tool-use patterns exploded in product use through 2024–2026; LangChain’s production framing: the LLM owns application control flow — not a hard-coded script.

try_it.title: Script vs agent
try_it.prompt: Goal: “Book a meeting if the calendar is free.” Choose path A (fixed script: always call calendar, then always email) vs path B (model picks next tool based on the last result). Which one is the agent pattern?
try_it.debrief: Chat answers once; agents keep deciding the next action until the goal is done (or they stop).

quiz.q: What makes a system an AI agent (per verified def)?
choices: It only returns one chat reply from a fixed template
The model decides what to do next — tools + looping on a goal

quiz.q: In LangChain’s production framing cited by Research, who owns application control flow?
choices: Only the human every single step

lessons.plain_def: An open standard for plugging AI assistants into tools and data sources through one shared protocol — like a USB-C port for AI apps — instead of a custom connector for every pair.
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Anthropic open-sourced MCP on Nov 25, 2024 (spec/docs at modelcontextprotocol.io) — one shared plug instead of a custom connector for every app↔tool pair.

try_it.title: Custom connectors vs one protocol
try_it.prompt: You have 4 assistants and 5 tools. Count the custom one-off connectors if every pair needs its own (4×5) vs one shared protocol each side speaks once. Which world is MCP aiming for?
try_it.debrief: MCP is the USB-C idea: speak the standard once, plug many tools without rewriting every pair.

lessons.plain_def: A fair-code workflow automation tool where you connect apps and AI steps on a visual canvas (or with code). Self-host for free, or use their cloud. Name = “nodemation,” said “n-eight-n.”
lessons.why_it_blew_up: Public launch October 2019 (Berlin, founder Jan Oberhauser); fair-code automation with a visual canvas made “wire AI + apps” accessible without a full custom backend.

try_it.title: Wire a three-node flow
try_it.prompt: On a fake canvas, connect: Webhook → AI step → Slack message. Say the flow out loud: “When X arrives, ask the model, then post Y.” Pronounce the product name correctly.
try_it.debrief: n8n is the canvas where APIs (and AI steps) become a visible workflow — self-host free or use cloud.

choices: A fair-code workflow automation tool with a visual canvas (or code)
